intro.en: Core surgical instruments tested as spotters in the MBBS practical examination, including scalpels, forceps, clamps, retractors, scissors, needle holders, probes, proctoscopes, and laparoscopic sets.

items.summary: A flat metallic scalpel handle with a narrow slotted tip designed to hold smaller surgical blades for delicate incisions.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Flat stainless steel handle with a slender slotted mounting tip.
Marked with the numeral 3 near the base.
Engineered to fit smaller surgical blades 10, 11, 12, and 15.
Features metric graduations on the handle for measuring skin lesions or incisions.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Making precise skin and subcuticular incisions in neck, face, and paediatric surgery.
Holding blade 11 for abscess drainage via Hiltons method or stab trochar puncture.
Holding blade 15 for minor surgeries like sebaceous cyst excision and dermoid enucleation.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Always mount and dismount blades using a needle holder or heavy artery forceps, never with bare fingers.
Held in a violin bow or dinner knife grip for long controlled incisions.
Held in a pencil grip only for delicate, short, or curved dissections.

viva.q: Which surgical blades fit a number 3 Bard-Parker handle?
viva.a: Blades numbered 10, 11, 12, and 15 fit the slot of a number 3 handle.

viva.q: What is blade number 11 specifically used for?
viva.a: Making stab incisions for abscess drainage, chest drain insertion, arteriotomies, and laparoscopic port entries.

viva.q: Why is bare-hand blade mounting strictly prohibited?
viva.a: It carries a severe risk of deep glove tears, sharp digital lacerations, and transmission of blood-borne viral pathogens.

image.brief: Metallic Bard-Parker handle number 3 shown on a sterile drape with its narrow slotted tip visible alongside detachable blades 11 and 15.

items.summary: A heavy metallic scalpel handle with a broad slotted tip designed to hold large surgical blades for major incisions.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Noticeably wider, thicker, and heavier than the number 3 handle.
Engraved with the numeral 4 near the base of the shaft.
Broad slotted mounting tip tailored to fit larger blades 20, 21, 22, 23, and 24.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Making long abdominal incisions in midline and paramedian laparotomies.
Cutting through tough deep fascia, aponeurosis, and anterior abdominal wall layers.
Making large skin flaps in radical mastectomy and limb amputations.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Blade 20 is the most commonly mounted blade, featuring a large curved cutting belly.
The belly of the blade, not the sharp tip, should divide the tissue in a continuous sweep.
The index finger is placed along the blunt spine of the handle to regulate downward cutting pressure.

viva.q: Which blades are compatible with a number 4 scalpel handle?
viva.a: Larger blades numbered 20, 21, 22, 23, and 24 fit the broad slot of a number 4 handle.

viva.q: How should the scalpel be held for a laparotomy incision?
viva.a: In a dinner knife grip with the index finger along the spine to control depth and pressure.

viva.q: Why is the pencil grip avoided for long abdominal incisions?
viva.a: The pencil grip scratches with the sharp tip, producing irregular jagged margins rather than a clean full-thickness cut.

image.brief: Heavy stainless steel Bard-Parker handle number 4 displayed beside a wide curved surgical blade number 20 on an instrument tray.

items.summary: A spring-action thumb forceps with interlocking sharp teeth at the tips used to grasp tough fibrous tissue without slipping.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Non-locking sprung tweezers with serrated finger grips on both shanks.
The working tips feature one tooth on one side interlocking with two teeth on the opposite side (1 into 2 teeth arrangement).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Grasping and steadying skin edges during cutaneous suturing.
Holding rectus sheath, linea alba, and external oblique aponeurosis during closure.
Grasping tough deep fascia and fibrotic wound margins.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Never used to grasp hollow viscera such as stomach, small intestine, colon, or bladder.
Strictly avoided on delicate blood vessels, bile ducts, and peripheral nerves due to puncture trauma.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Held like a pencil between thumb and index-middle fingers of the non-dominant hand.
Interlocking teeth maintain a secure grip with minimal crushing force compared to flat forceps.

viva.q: What tissues are appropriately handled using toothed dissecting forceps?
viva.a: Tough collagenous structures including skin, subcutaneous fibrous bands, rectus sheath, and aponeurotic fascia.

viva.q: Why are toothed forceps forbidden on hollow viscera?
viva.a: The sharp teeth puncture epithelial and muscular layers, causing transmural tears, necrosis, and anastomotic leakage.

viva.q: What is the mechanical advantage of the toothed tip on skin?
viva.a: Sharp teeth hold dermis securely without slipping, avoiding the crush damage caused by heavily squeezing non-toothed forceps.

image.brief: Stainless steel toothed dissecting forceps with tips slightly open showing the classic 1 into 2 interlocking tooth configuration.

items.summary: A spring-action thumb forceps with transversely serrated blunt tips for atraumatic manipulation of delicate visceral tissues.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Sprung thumb forceps without sharp teeth at the tips.
Both inner jaw surfaces have fine transverse serrations and blunt rounded tips.
Shanks have ribbed finger rests for tactile control.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Handling stomach, bowel wall, and visceral peritoneum during abdominal surgery.
Holding blood vessels and vascular pedicles during dissection and ligation.
Manipulating soft tissues, lymph nodes, and delicate subcutaneous fat.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Because it lacks interlocking teeth, slippery tissues may slip out.
Excessive pinching force must be avoided to prevent crushing delicate tissues.
Held in the non-dominant hand using a gentle pencil grip.

viva.q: Where are plain non-toothed forceps preferred over toothed forceps?
viva.a: When handling delicate hollow organs, intestine, peritoneum, blood vessels, and soft visceral tissues.

viva.q: Why is non-toothed forceps poor for holding skin edges?
viva.a: Skin slips easily, tempting the surgeon to pinch tightly, which crushes dermal capillaries and causes edge necrosis.

viva.q: How does the surgeon prevent tissue crush with non-toothed forceps?
viva.a: By applying gentle, measured fingertip pressure just enough to steady the organ without compressing its microvasculature.

image.brief: Non-toothed dissecting forceps open on a sterile cloth showing fine transverse serrated ridges on the blunt rounded tips.

items.summary: A ratcheted forceps with expanding jaws ending in multiple fine interlocking teeth designed to grip tough fascial margins and flaps.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Ring handles, ratchet lock mechanism, and box joint.
Blades curve inwards at the tip to form an expanded transverse jaw.
Tips feature multiple fine interlocking teeth (usually 4 into 5 or 5 into 6 teeth) resembling a comb.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Holding and elevating skin flaps during mastectomy and neck dissection.
Grasping rectus sheath, linea alba, and aponeurosis during abdominal closure.
Holding the base of the appendix or traction on subcutaneous fascial margins.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Produces localized crush injury; should not be placed on viable stomach, bowel, or bladder wall.
Ideal for tissue that will be excised or tough aponeurotic layers that resist damage.

viva.q: Describe the tip architecture of an Allis tissue forceps.
viva.a: Jaws expand transversely and terminate in multiple fine, sharp interlocking comb-like teeth.

viva.q: Why should Allis forceps not be clamped onto the small intestine?
viva.a: Its sharp interlocking teeth and crushing ratchet cause mucosal laceration, wall necrosis, and perforation.

viva.q: Name a procedure where Allis forceps is used to handle large skin flaps.
viva.a: Modified radical mastectomy, where it lifts skin flaps off the underlying breast tissue and pectoralis major muscle.

image.brief: Allis tissue forceps shown locked on the first ratchet notch with magnified view of the interlocking comb-like teeth at the jaws.

items.summary: An atraumatic ratcheted forceps with smooth fenestrated triangular loops designed to grasp tubular viscera safely.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Ring handles, ratchet lock, and long shanks with a box joint.
Jaws expand into a fenestrated triangular or oval loop.
Terminal grasping bars are broad, smooth, and completely devoid of teeth or sharp serrations.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Holding the vermiform appendix during appendicectomy without puncturing the inflamed wall.
Grasping and manipulating fallopian tubes, ureters, and spermatic cord structures.
Holding small bowel loops, stomach wall, and lymph node packets atraumatically.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The broad fenestrated tips encircle the tubular organ and distribute mechanical holding force evenly.
Considered the standard atraumatic visceral holding forceps in general surgery.

viva.q: What makes Babcock forceps safe for gripping hollow organs?
viva.a: The broad rounded fenestrated jaws distribute pressure over a large contact area without teeth or sharp edges.

viva.q: Name three tubular organs routinely handled with Babcock forceps.
viva.a: The vermiform appendix, the fallopian tube, and the ureter.

viva.q: How does Babcock forceps differ from Allis forceps?
viva.a: Babcock has smooth rounded fenestrated tips without teeth, whereas Allis has multiple sharp interlocking teeth.

image.brief: Babcock tissue forceps displayed open showing the characteristic fenestrated triangular loops with smooth horizontal bars.

items.summary: A ratcheted clamp with transversely serrated blunt-nosed jaws used to compress bleeding blood vessels for haemostasis.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Ring handles with a multi-step ratchet lock mechanism.
Sturdy tapering jaws with transverse serrations along the entire inner gripping face.
Available in straight and curved patterns, usually 15 to 20 cm in length.
Lacks teeth at the tip, distinguishing it from Kocher forceps.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Clamping bleeding blood vessels prior to ligature or diathermy coagulation.
Performing blunt dissection through loose connective tissue planes.
Holding stay sutures and tags during vascular or bowel surgery.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Curved artery forceps allows the surgeon to visualize the vessel tip and pass a ligature smoothly underneath.
Only the tip of the bleeding vessel should be grasped to prevent crushing surrounding nerves.

viva.q: What is the primary function of Spencer Wells artery forceps?
viva.a: Clamping bleeding blood vessels to arrest haemorrhage prior to definitive ligation or electrocoagulation.

viva.q: Why is curved artery forceps often preferred over straight?
viva.a: The curve provides superior visibility of the bleeding point and facilitates slipping a ligature loop beneath the tip.

viva.q: Why should you avoid taking large bites of surrounding tissue with the clamp?
viva.a: Large bites crush adjacent nerves and healthy tissue, leading to necrosis and loose ligatures.

image.brief: Straight and curved Spencer Wells artery forceps shown side by side with ratchets locked, highlighting transverse serrations.

items.summary: A delicate lightweight ratcheted forceps with fine tapering jaws for clamping small bleeding vessels in sensitive areas.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Delicate, miniature version of Spencer Wells forceps, typically 12.5 cm long.
Fine pointed jaws with delicate transverse serrations along the gripping face.
Available in straight or curved patterns with fine ratchets.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Clamping tiny bleeders in thyroidectomy, plastic surgery, and paediatric procedures.
Tagging and handling fine monofilament sutures such as 5-0 or 6-0 prolene.
Delicate dissection around fragile nerves and superficial vessels.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Never use mosquito forceps to clamp thick pedicles or heavy fascia.
Forcing delicate jaws against thick tissue will bend or spring the instrument.

viva.q: How does a mosquito forceps differ from a standard Spencer Wells forceps?
viva.a: It is much smaller and lighter with extremely fine, pointed jaws designed for pinpoint haemostasis.

viva.q: Name two operations where mosquito forceps is routinely employed.
viva.a: Thyroidectomy and cleft lip or palate repair.

viva.q: What happens if a mosquito forceps is clamped on tough abdominal fascia?
viva.a: The fine delicate jaws will permanently distort, spring out of alignment, or fracture.

image.brief: Delicate curved Halsted mosquito forceps lying beside a standard artery forceps to demonstrate its fine profile and miniature size.

items.summary: A heavy ratcheted clamp with transverse serrations and interlocking sharp 1x2 teeth at the tip to grip tough vascular pedicles securely.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Heavy, rigid shanks with a sturdy box joint and ratchet.
Transverse serrations along the full length of the jaws.
Distal tips end in sharp interlocking 1 into 2 teeth.
Manufactured in straight and curved varieties from 14 to 20 cm.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Clamping heavy vascular pedicles like the superior thyroid pedicle, broad ligament, or omentum.
Crushing the base of the appendix before ligation in appendicectomy.
Holding the edges of the rectus sheath during abdominal wound closure.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The distal teeth prevent slippery high-pressure pedicles from slipping out of the jaws.
Because it is severely crushing, it should only be used on tissue that will be excised or tough fascia.

viva.q: What design feature distinguishes Kocher forceps from Spencer Wells forceps?
viva.a: Kocher forceps possesses sharp 1 into 2 interlocking teeth at the distal jaw tips.

viva.q: Why are the distal teeth beneficial on heavy vascular pedicles?
viva.a: The teeth prevent dense, slippery pedicles from sliding out during ligature placement and tie down.

viva.q: What role does Kocher forceps play during appendicectomy?
viva.a: It is applied across the base of the appendix to crush the lumen and displace mucosa before ligation.

image.brief: Straight Kocher haemostatic clamp with jaws slightly ajar displaying the prominent 1 into 2 teeth at the tips.

items.summary: A ratcheted clamp with sharp inward-curving pointed pincers used to secure sterile drapes around the operative field.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Ring handles with a ratchet lock and short crossed shanks.
Distal ends curve inward into sharply pointed, needle-like pincers that overlap when closed.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Securing sterile drapes to each other and anchoring them to the patient skin.
Fixing electrocautery leads, suction tubing, and camera cables to sterile drapes.
Occasionally used for bone traction in mandibular or rib fractures.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Accidental skin puncture or haematoma if placed through excessive skin depth.
Contamination risk: once unclamped, the penetrating tips are contaminated and must not be reapplied to the field.

viva.q: What is the primary function of the Backhaus towel clip?
viva.a: Securing operative drapes around the surgical site to maintain a stable sterile barrier.

viva.q: Why is a towel clip considered contaminated once released from drapes?
viva.a: Its sharp points penetrate through drapes and touch the skin; moving it transfers unsterile organisms across the field.

viva.q: What precaution is taken when applying towel clips under general anaesthesia?
viva.a: Ensure that deep underlying subcutaneous tissues or sensitive anatomical structures are not pinched.

image.brief: Metallic Backhaus towel clip showing ring handles, ratchet, and sharply curved pointed pincers locked on the first tooth.

items.summary: A long ratcheted forceps with large fenestrated oval jaws used for preoperative skin preparation and deep cavity swabbing.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Long instrument (around 25 cm) with ring handles, box joint, and ratchet lock.
Jaws expand into large oval loops with central fenestrations and transverse serrations on the inner rim.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Painting the surgical operative field with antiseptic solutions like povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine.
Holding gauze sponges to mop blood and clear vision in deep cavities during laparotomy.
Grasping the fundus of the gallbladder during open cholecystectomy.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Gauze swabs must be folded with raw edges tucked inside so loose cotton threads are not left in the wound.
The long shank provides deep reach into the pelvis and subdiaphragmatic spaces.

viva.q: Name the two primary uses of Rampley sponge-holding forceps.
viva.a: Skin antiseptic preparation (painting) prior to surgery and holding gauze swabs for deep field haemostasis.

viva.q: Why are the oval jaws fenestrated?
viva.a: The fenestrations hold bulky gauze swabs securely without slipping or crushing the cotton.

viva.q: Which viscera is commonly grasped with Rampley forceps during cholecystectomy?
viva.a: The gallbladder fundus is grasped to exert traction and expose Calots triangle.

image.brief: Long stainless steel Rampley sponge-holding forceps grasping a folded sterile gauze swab between its oval fenestrated jaws.

items.summary: A long atraumatic clamp with flexible, longitudinally grooved blades used to occlude bowel lumen and prevent spillage during resection.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Long, slender, flexible blades that bow slightly outwards and touch only at the tips when loosely closed.
Inner surfaces have fine longitudinal ridges (striations) running parallel to the blades.
Available in straight and curved patterns with multi-notch ratchet handles.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Temporary occlusion of stomach, small intestine, or colon during resection and anastomosis to prevent enteric spillage.
Holding bowel ends in alignment while suturing an end-to-end or side-to-side anastomosis.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Longitudinal serrations compress fewer intramural vessels, preserving microcirculation along the cut bowel edge.
Should only be engaged on the first or second ratchet catch to avoid ischemic transmural crushing.

viva.q: Why do Doyen clamps have longitudinal rather than transverse serrations?
viva.a: Longitudinal grooves parallel the bowel blood supply, compressing fewer submucosal vessels and preventing ischemia.

viva.q: What is the primary objective of applying Doyen clamps during gut anastomosis?
viva.a: To prevent spillage of dirty luminal contents and faecal organisms into the sterile peritoneal cavity.

viva.q: Why should a Doyen clamp never be tightened beyond the second ratchet notch?
viva.a: Excessive closing pressure crushes bowel wall layers, leading to mucosal necrosis and anastomotic dehiscence.

image.brief: Curved Doyen intestinal clamp shown partially open displaying its long flexible blades with fine longitudinal ridges.

items.summary: A heavy lever-action crushing clamp used to crush gastrointestinal walls and seal mucosal vessels before division.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Heavy, rigid instrument without finger rings; features a hinged lever arm and locking pin mechanism.
Thick, solid, longitudinally grooved jaws produce immense mechanical crushing force.
Manufactured in large gastric and smaller intestinal sizes.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Crushing the stomach wall and duodenum during partial or subtotal gastrectomy.
Crushing the colon before transection during colectomy, creating a closed stump.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The immense pressure crushes mucosa and seals submucosal vessels, preventing bleeding and contamination.
Applied only to portions of bowel that will be resected or invaginated by seromuscular sutures.

viva.q: What is the mechanical principle of the Payr clamp?
viva.a: A compound lever mechanism that delivers high crushing force to seal lumen and haemostatically flatten submucosal vessels.

viva.q: Name a classic operation where Payr clamps are applied.
viva.a: Partial or subtotal gastrectomy for gastric cancer or complicated peptic ulcer disease.

viva.q: Why is a Payr clamp never applied to bowel that will remain in continuity?
viva.a: Because its heavy crushing pressure destroys all tissue layers, causing permanent transmural necrosis.

image.brief: Heavy stainless steel Payr crushing clamp showing its compound lever arm, locking screw pin, and thick flat jaws.

items.summary: A handheld L-shaped retractor with a flat right-angled blade used to retract superficial wound edges in soft tissue operations.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Flat metallic handle terminating in a single perpendicular right-angled blade.
The blade end has a slight upward lip to prevent tissue from slipping off.
Manufactured in various blade depths from 2 cm to 6 cm.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Retracting skin and subcutaneous fat in hernia repairs and appendicectomies.
Retracting soft tissue flaps in thyroidectomy, parotidectomy, and varicose vein surgery.
Excision of benign lumps like lipomas, fibroadenomas, and sebaceous cysts.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Handheld and non-self-retaining, requiring steady traction by an assistant.
Excessive or jerky retraction must be avoided to prevent skin edge bruising and ischaemia.

viva.q: What category of retractor does Langenbeck belong to?
viva.a: A handheld, non-self-retaining, right-angled superficial soft tissue retractor.

viva.q: In which common operations is the Langenbeck retractor routinely used?
viva.a: Inguinal hernia repair, appendicectomy, thyroidectomy, and excision of subcutaneous lumps.

viva.q: What complication can arise from rough assistant retraction with this instrument?
viva.a: Skin edge crush injury, fat necrosis, and postoperative wound edge devitalisation.

image.brief: Stainless steel Langenbeck retractor displayed showing its flat handle and smooth right-angled perpendicular blade.

items.summary: A double-ended handheld retractor with a shallow hook at one end and a broad fenestrated blade at the other for layered wound exposure.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Double-ended flat metal strip.
One end has a curved shallow hook flange for superficial skin retraction.
The opposite end has a broad, right-angled blade with a central oval fenestration for deeper layers.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Retracting the abdominal wall in appendicectomy through a McBurney or Lanz gridiron incision.
Layer-by-layer retraction of external and internal oblique muscles in hernia surgery.
Minor exploratory laparotomy wound retraction.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The fenestration in the broad blade reduces instrument weight and provides friction against moist muscles.
Reversible design allows quick switching between superficial and deep exposure.

viva.q: Describe the two ends of a Czerny retractor.
viva.a: One end features a shallow hooked lip for skin, while the opposite end has a wide right-angled fenestrated blade for deep muscle.

viva.q: Which emergency surgery frequently utilizes Czerny retractors in India?
viva.a: Open appendicectomy performed through a McBurney or Lanz incision.

viva.q: What is the purpose of the window on the broad blade?
viva.a: It reduces instrument weight, prevents muscle slipping, and allows visualization of underlying tissue.

image.brief: Double-ended Czerny retractor showing the hook flange at one pole and broad fenestrated rectangular blade at the opposite pole.

items.summary: A deep handheld retractor curved like a question mark, engineered to hold back viscera without injuring delicate organ capsules.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Smooth, polished steel ribbon bent into a wide sweeping curve resembling a question mark.
Features a broad curved handle for the assistant to maintain firm ergonomic traction.
Available in multiple blade widths from narrow (2.5 cm) to broad (7.5 cm).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Retracting the liver, stomach, and colon during upper abdominal surgery like cholecystectomy and gastrectomy.
Deep pelvic retraction during low anterior resection, rectal excision, and pelvic lymphadenectomy.
Retracting chest wall structures during thoracotomy.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The sweeping curved contour distributes traction forces broadly across organ surfaces, minimizing tears.
The assistant must hold it steadily without rocking, which can tear the fragile hepatic or splenic capsule.

viva.q: What is the primary role of the Deaver retractor?
viva.a: Deep visceral retraction in abdominal and pelvic surgery, especially elevating the liver or displacing bowel loops.

viva.q: Why is its curved ribbon profile safer than a sharp right-angled retractor?
viva.a: The gentle sweeping curve eliminates focal pressure points, reducing the danger of tearing fragile solid organs.

viva.q: What organ capsule is particularly vulnerable to injury during upper abdominal retraction?
viva.a: The hepatic capsule (Glissons capsule) and the splenic capsule can be torn by careless retractor movement.

image.brief: Wide curved stainless steel Deaver retractor showing its question-mark curve and ergonomic hook handle.

items.summary: A heavy right-angled handheld retractor with an incurved terminal lip designed to retract full-thickness abdominal wall muscles.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Sturdy flat handle connected to a wide right-angled rectangular blade.
The distal edge features a prominent inward-curved lip or flange.
Substantially larger and heavier than a Langenbeck retractor.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Retracting the thick muscular abdominal wall during exploratory laparotomies.
Retracting the pelvic wall in colorectal and gynaecological operations.
Exposure of retroperitoneal structures such as abdominal aorta, kidneys, and inferior vena cava.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The inward-curved terminal lip hooks behind the posterior rectus sheath, preventing slipping under tension.
Usually held with a moist gauze pad between the metal blade and the abdominal wall to protect muscle.

viva.q: What structural feature prevents the Morris retractor from slipping out during traction?
viva.a: The prominent inward-curved lip on the distal edge of the blade firmly hooks behind the abdominal wall layers.

viva.q: How does Morris retractor differ from Langenbeck retractor?
viva.a: Morris is much larger with a broader blade and an incurved lip, designed for heavy abdominal wall retraction.

viva.q: Name two procedures where Morris retractors are routinely used.
viva.a: Midline exploratory laparotomy and open abdominal aortic surgery.

image.brief: Heavy Morris retractor displaying its broad right-angled blade and characteristic inward-curled retaining lip.

items.summary: A self-retaining frame retractor with adjustable lateral blades and a detachable central suprapubic blade for broad abdominal exposure.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Heavy metallic frame featuring a fixed lateral wire blade and a sliding lateral wire blade on a notched track.
Fitted with a thumbscrew or ratchet to lock the lateral blades apart.
Equipped with a detachable curved central blade for suprapubic or bladder retraction.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Maintaining wide continuous exposure during major laparotomies, gastrectomies, and colectomies.
Deep pelvic exposure in radical cystectomy, rectal resection, and gynaecological oncology.
Frees assistants from holding handheld retractors during long operations.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Moist laparotomy sponges must always be placed beneath the lateral blades to prevent pressure necrosis.
Over-spreading the lateral blades can compress the femoral nerve against the pelvic brim, causing postoperative quadriceps weakness.

viva.q: What are the components of a complete Balfour retractor assembly?
viva.a: A crossbar frame with one fixed and one sliding lateral blade, a locking mechanism, and a detachable central bladder blade.

viva.q: Why must moist abdominal sponges be placed between the blades and wound margins?
viva.a: To cushion the muscular edges, distribute pressure evenly, and prevent ischemic necrosis and nerve injury.

viva.q: Which major nerve is at risk of neuropraxia if the blades are opened excessively?
viva.a: The femoral nerve, which can be compressed against the lateral pelvic wall causing postoperative leg weakness.

image.brief: Balfour self-retaining retractor assembly displaying two lateral wire blades on a track and the attachable curved central blade.

items.summary: Heavy surgical scissors with thick beveled blades and rounded tips used to divide tough fascial and fibrous tissue planes.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Robust construction with thick blades roughly equal in length to the shanks (1 to 1 blade-to-shank ratio).
Beveled cutting edges with blunt rounded tips.
Manufactured in straight (suture cutting) and curved (fascial dissection) forms.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Curved Mayo scissors cut tough fibrous structures like rectus sheath, linea alba, and dense scar adhesions.
Straight Mayo scissors cut heavy suture materials, surgical drains, and prosthetic meshes.
Dividing thick vascular pedicles and tough ligaments.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Curved Mayo scissors should never be used to cut paper, gauze, or wire, which blunts the blades.
Always inspect the screw hinge: loose screws cause scissors to fold rather than cut tissue.

viva.q: What tissues are curved Mayo scissors designed to cut?
viva.a: Tough fibrous tissues such as rectus sheath, linea alba, deep fascia, tendons, and dense scar tissue.

viva.q: How does Mayo scissors differ structurally from Metzenbaum scissors?
viva.a: Mayo has thick, heavy blades roughly equal in length to the shanks, whereas Metzenbaum has slender blades with long shanks.

viva.q: What is straight Mayo scissors routinely used for on the operating table?
viva.a: Cutting heavy non-absorbable sutures, ligatures, wound drains, and prosthetic mesh.

image.brief: Curved Mayo dissecting scissors shown partially open displaying heavy beveled cutting blades and rounded tips.

items.summary: Slender surgical scissors with long shanks and short delicate blades engineered exclusively for dissecting soft tissue planes.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Long, slender shanks paired with relatively short, delicate blades (shank-to-blade ratio around 2 to 1 or greater).
Blades are thin with smooth rounded blunt tips; typically curved.
Lightweight instrument designed for fine fingertip tactile control.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Fine blunt and sharp dissection in soft tissue planes, hernia sac dissection, and mobilizing bowel mesentery.
Careful isolation of cystic duct and cystic artery in cholecystectomy.
Dividing fine vascular adhesions and dissecting around nerves and major vessels.

blocks.title: Contraindications
bullets: Never used to cut skin, tough fascia, aponeurosis, suture threads, or prosthetic mesh.
Cutting dense materials springs the delicate hinge and permanently ruins the micro-aligned cutting edge.

viva.q: What is the primary surgical role of Metzenbaum scissors?
viva.a: Fine blunt and sharp dissection of delicate soft tissue planes, visceral mobilization, and vessel skeletonization.

viva.q: Why should Metzenbaum scissors never be used to cut suture material?
viva.a: Sutures blunt the fine micro-edges and distort the alignment of the slender blades, ruining them for tissue dissection.

viva.q: What anatomical proportion distinguishes Metzenbaum scissors?
viva.a: The shanks are long and slender while the cutting blades are short and thin.

image.brief: Slender curved Metzenbaum scissors displayed open showing the long shanks and fine delicate blades with blunt tips.

items.summary: A ratcheted instrument with short, thick, cross-hatched serrated jaws and a central groove designed to grip curved surgical needles firmly.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Ring handles with a precise multi-notch ratchet and long shanks.
Jaws are short and thick with cross-hatched (criss-cross) serrations, often featuring golden handles denoting tungsten carbide inserts.
A shallow longitudinal groove runs down the centre of the jaws to seat curved needles securely without rocking.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Holding curved surgical needles securely during suturing of abdominal wall, fascia, bowel, and skin.
Assisting in instrument-tied surgical knots in deep or confined spaces.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Needle should be clamped at the junction of its proximal two thirds and distal one third.
Never grasp the swaged eye end (causes thread pullout) or the sharp needle tip (blunts the point).
Held with the thumb and fourth finger in the rings, index finger extended along the shank to guide precision.

viva.q: How do the jaws of a needle holder differ from an artery forceps?
viva.a: A needle holder has much shorter, thicker jaws with criss-cross serrations and a central groove, preventing needle rotation.

viva.q: Where should the needle holder grasp a curved needle?
viva.a: At the junction of the proximal two thirds and distal one third of the needle shaft.

viva.q: What do golden ring handles indicate on a needle holder?
viva.a: They signify hard tungsten carbide jaw inserts that resist wear, slipping, and needle deformation.

image.brief: Mayo-Hegar needle holder with gold ring handles open to show short jaws with criss-cross serrations and central longitudinal groove.

items.summary: A malleable metallic probe paired with a channeled director used to evaluate fistulous tracts and guide division of overlying tissue.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: The probe is a slender, malleable silver or steel rod ending in a smooth olive-shaped bulbous tip.
The grooved director is a flat metal instrument with a central longitudinal channel running down its shaft.
The wide spade-shaped handle of the director features a heart-shaped notch (butterfly retractor).

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Probing fistula-in-ano to trace the tract from the external skin opening to the internal anal opening.
Exploring branchial or thyroglossal sinuses and pilonidal sinus tracts.
The grooved channel guides a scalpel or bistoury to slit open the fistula tract safely (fistulotomy).
The butterfly end acts as a tongue retractor during frenulotomy for tongue-tie (ankyloglossia).

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Must be guided with gentle fingertip touch; forceful probing easily creates a false passage.
Silver composition allows the probe to be bent manually to conform to curved anatomical tracts.

viva.q: What is the greatest danger during probing of a fistula-in-ano?
viva.a: Applying excessive force, which punctures the fibrous tract wall and creates an artificial false passage.

viva.q: What is Goodsalls rule for fistula-in-ano?
viva.a: External openings anterior to the transverse anal line track straight; posterior openings curve towards the posterior midline.

viva.q: What is the function of the butterfly notch on the director handle?
viva.a: It straddles and protects the lingual frenulum while shielding the deep tongue vessels during division of a tongue tie.

image.brief: Malleable silver fistula probe alongside a steel grooved director showing the central gutter and notched butterfly tail.

items.summary: A rigid metallic tubular speculum fitted with a rounded obturator used for direct visual inspection of the anal canal and lower rectum.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Hollow stainless steel cylinder with a flared proximal rim and an ergonomic downward-angled handle.
Contains a removable solid central obturator with a smooth, bullet-shaped rounded tip.
Length is approximately 7 to 8 cm with an internal diameter of 1.5 to 2 cm.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Visualising internal haemorrhoids and assessing degree of mucosal prolapse.
Detecting anal fissures, hypertrophied anal papillae, and internal fistula orifices.
Taking mucosal biopsies from suspicious low rectal ulcers or tumours.
Assisting in rubber band ligation and sclerotherapy of internal piles.

blocks.title: Steps of examination
bullets: Patient placed in left lateral Sims position with buttocks at the edge of the examining couch.
Perform mandatory digital rectal examination to lubricate the canal and exclude obstructing masses.
Lubricate proctoscope with lignocaine jelly and insert pointing initially towards the umbilicus, then backwards into the sacral hollow.
Withdraw obturator, advance light source, and inspect the mucosa systematically as the barrel is slowly withdrawn.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Internal haemorrhoids prolapse into the lumen at the classic 3, 7, and 11 o clock positions.
Never insert the proctoscope without its obturator; the sharp rim would lacerate the anal mucosa.

viva.q: Why must digital rectal examination precede proctoscopy?
viva.a: To assess sphincter tone, rule out painful fissures or obstructing tumours, and lubricate the canal for safe entry.

viva.q: What are the three primary anatomical sites for internal haemorrhoids?
viva.a: At the 3, 7, and 11 o clock positions, corresponding to the terminal branches of the superior rectal artery.

viva.q: Why is the obturator essential during insertion?
viva.a: The rounded bullet tip dilates the anal canal smoothly without tearing the mucosa, which a bare hollow rim would do.

image.brief: Metallic cylindrical Kelly proctoscope shown with its bullet-shaped obturator partly pulled out of the barrel alongside the handle.

items.summary: A rigid metallic tubular instrument with obturator, optical eyepiece, light channel, and bellows used to examine the rectum and rectosigmoid junction.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Long hollow metal tube (25 to 30 cm) graduated in centimetres along its outer shaft.
Equipped with a solid removable obturator, an attachable glass viewing window, and an illumination fiberoptic channel.
Fitted with a rubber double-bulb insufflator to puff air and distend the rectal lumen.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Diagnosing carcinoma of the rectum and recto-sigmoid junction up to 25 cm from the anal verge.
Evaluating ulcerative colitis, proctitis, rectal polyps, and radiation injury.
Taking targeted punch biopsies and performing decompression of sigmoid volvulus.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Perforation of the bowel wall, most common at the recto-sigmoid junction (12 to 15 cm) where the bowel curves sharply anteriorly.
Bleeding from biopsy sites or tearing of friable inflamed mucosa.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Once past the anal canal (around 5 cm), the obturator is withdrawn and the scope is advanced strictly under direct vision.
Never push against resistance: gentle air insufflation should open the lumen ahead of the scope tip.

viva.q: What is the working length of a standard rigid sigmoidoscope?
viva.a: Typically 25 to 30 centimetres, enabling inspection of the anal canal, rectum, and lower sigmoid colon.

viva.q: Where is the bowel most vulnerable to perforation during rigid sigmoidoscopy?
viva.a: At the recto-sigmoid junction between 12 and 15 centimetres, where the lumen angles sharply anterosuperiorly.

viva.q: Why is the obturator removed once the scope enters the rectal ampulla?
viva.a: All further advancement must occur under direct vision with light and air insufflation to prevent blind perforation.

image.brief: Graduated 30 cm rigid metal sigmoidoscope tube with attached glass magnifying lens, rubber air bellows, and removable obturator.

items.summary: A spring-loaded needle with an outer sharp bevel and an inner blunt stylet designed for safe blind creation of pneumoperitoneum in laparoscopy.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Metallic needle with a proximal luer-lock hub and a two-way stopcock.
Contains a spring-loaded blunt-ended inner stylet that projects beyond the outer sharp beveled needle tip.
When pushed against resistance, the blunt stylet retracts into the shaft, exposing the sharp cutting bevel.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Puncturing the anterior abdominal wall (subumbilical or Palmers point) to infuse carbon dioxide for pneumoperitoneum.
Initial step in closed-entry laparoscopic surgery.

blocks.title: Safety tests for correct entry
bullets: Saline drop test: a drop of saline on the open hub disappears inside when the abdominal wall is lifted.
Aspiration test: syringe aspiration must yield neither blood, bowel contents, nor urine.
Syringe injection test: saline injects smoothly with negligible resistance and cannot be re-aspirated.
Initial insufflation pressure test: starting pressure should be low, below 10 mmHg at a low flow rate.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Puncture of major retroperitoneal vessels (aorta, inferior vena cava, common iliac vessels).
Perforation of stomach, transverse colon, or mesenteric veins.

viva.q: What is the safety mechanism of the Veress needle?
viva.a: The spring-loaded inner blunt stylet retracts during fascial resistance and springs forward upon entering the peritoneal cavity, shielding viscera.

viva.q: What is Palmers point and when is it preferred for Veress needle insertion?
viva.a: Located 3 cm below the left costal margin in the midclavicular line, used when previous midline laparotomy poses umbilical adhesion risk.

viva.q: Describe the saline drop test on a Veress needle.
viva.a: Saline placed on the hub is sucked into the abdomen by negative intra-abdominal pressure when the abdominal wall is lifted.

image.brief: Spring-loaded Veress needle displaying the stopcock hub and close-up of the bevel with the inner blunt safety rod projecting forward.

items.summary: A port assembly consisting of a central pointed trocar and an outer hollow sleeve with a gas valve, establishing access for laparoscopic instruments.

blocks.title: How to recognise it
bullets: Hollow outer cannula fitted with a gas-sealing valve, side insufflation stopcock, and silicone gasket.
Central removable trocar with a sharp pyramidal, conical, or optical clear plastic tip.
Available in standard 5 mm, 10 mm, and 12 mm diameters.

blocks.title: Uses
bullets: Establishing primary and secondary access ports through the abdominal wall in laparoscopic surgery.
Permits passage of laparoscope camera, graspers, scissors, clips, and staplers while maintaining pneumoperitoneum.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Laceration of inferior epigastric vessels during secondary lateral port placement.
Bowel perforation or vascular injury during primary blind trocar insertion.
Port-site incisional hernia if fascial defects of 10 mm or greater are left unclosed.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Secondary ports should always be inserted under direct visual guidance with the laparoscope camera.
Transillumination of the abdominal wall helps identify and avoid the inferior epigastric vessels.

viva.q: What is the Hasson open technique for trocar entry?
viva.a: A small cut-down incision through fascia and peritoneum under direct vision, inserting a blunt cannula secured with stay sutures.

viva.q: Why must trocar sites 10 mm or larger have their fascial defect closed with sutures?
viva.a: To prevent bowel or omental herniation through the unclosed fascial port, causing a Richter hernia or strangulation.

viva.q: How can inferior epigastric vessel injury be avoided during lateral port placement?
viva.a: By transilluminating the abdominal wall with the laparoscope and placing ports lateral to the rectus abdominis muscle under direct vision.

image.brief: Laparoscopic 10 mm trocar and cannula disassembled showing the pointed central stylet, outer sleeve, and gas stopcock valve.
